content: The relationship between physical activity and cardiovascular disease mortality is well-established, with evidence supporting an inverse association. This relationship extends beyond the currently recommended levels of physical activity, demonstrating a dose-response effect. A meta-analysis of 48 prospective studies examining total, leisure, and occupational physical activity further supports this dose-response relationship, indicating that higher levels of physical activity are associated with greater health benefits. Previous WHO guidelines recommended that aerobic activity should be performed in bouts of at least 10 minutes. However, new evidence from device-based assessments shows that physical activity of any duration, regardless of a minimum threshold, is associated with improved health outcomes, including reduced all-cause mortality. This evidence has led to the removal of the 10-minute bout requirement in updated recommendations. While higher levels of physical activity are consistently associated with a lower risk of site-specific cancers, there is insufficient evidence to determine the exact levels of activity required for risk reduction due to variability in study methodologies and exposure classifications. Importantly, there is no evidence to suggest a lower threshold below which physical activity ceases to provide benefits, indicating that any level of physical activity can reduce the risk of site-specific cancers. Further research is needed to better understand the dose-response relationship and to establish consistent measures for physical activity and its health outcomes. This will help refine future guidelines and identify minimal effective doses and maximum safety thresholds for different population subgroups. There is substantial evidence linking physical activity to various measures of adiposity, weight management, and maintaining a healthy weight status. However, there is insufficient evidence to describe the dose-response relationship or identify a specific threshold of effect for adults aged 18–64 years. Additional research is required to inform future guidelines. Physical activity, including both acute bouts and regular engagement, has been shown to improve sleep quality and health-related quality of life in adults. However, there is insufficient evidence to describe the dose-response relationship between physical activity and individual mental and cognitive health outcomes. Similarly, more evidence is needed to clarify the relationship between the volume and intensity of aerobic physical activity, muscle-strengthening exercises, and specific health outcomes. The WHO guidelines emphasize that higher levels of physical activity are associated with greater health benefits, although the relative benefits plateau at higher levels of activity. There is high-certainty evidence that increased physical activity reduces the risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, cardiovascular disease incidence, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes, with no increased risk of harm. Moderate-certainty evidence supports the association between physical activity of any duration and improved health outcomes, leading to the removal of the prior requirement for 10-minute bouts of aerobic activity. Additionally, higher amounts of physical activity are associated with more favorable measures of adiposity and weight management in adults, with a low risk of harm. Engaging in 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, or an equivalent amount, significantly reduces the risk of multiple health outcomes. Risk reduction continues beyond 300 minutes per week but begins to plateau. Both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities provide health benefits, with optimal outcomes achieved by meeting recommended levels of both types of activity. Muscle-strengthening activities, performed independently of aerobic activity, are associated with lower all-cause mortality risk. Evidence supports recommending muscle-strengthening exercises at least two days per week for additional health benefits. However, there is insufficient evidence to specify the optimal duration of such activities. Physical activity across different domains (e.g., leisure, transport, occupational) can provide health benefits, but there is insufficient evidence to differentiate the effects of these domains on various health outcomes. For example, the association between physical activity and cancer risk or type 2 diabetes incidence may vary by domain, but more research is needed to clarify these relationships. For mental health outcomes, various types of physical activity, including aerobic exercise, walking, muscle-strengthening activities, and yoga, have been shown to reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety. Resistance exercise interventions, in particular, have demonstrated moderately large reductions in depression symptoms and small reductions in anxiety symptoms compared to control conditions. High levels of occupational physical activity are associated with reduced risks of certain cancers, coronary heart disease, and type 2 diabetes. However, they may also increase the risk of osteoarthritis, poor sleep quality, and all-cause mortality among males (but not females). There is insufficient evidence to determine the relationship between occupational physical activity and adiposity, weight gain prevention, mental health, and health-related quality of life. The WHO guidelines recommend limiting sedentary behavior to reduce health risks. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity, including light-intensity activity, provides health benefits. Adults should aim to exceed the recommended levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity to mitigate the adverse effects of high levels of sedentary behavior. Greater time spent in sedentary behavior is associated with poor health outcomes, including higher all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, cancer mortality, and the incidence of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Evidence from meta-analyses and reviews supports these associations, even after adjusting for physical activity levels. There is limited evidence on the adverse effects of reducing sedentary time, but expert opinion suggests that replacing sedentary behavior with light-intensity physical activity is unlikely to increase the risk of injury. Further research is needed to better understand the relationship between sedentary behavior and health outcomes and to inform future guidelines.
